subtype: Approach: rehearsing in front of a mirror or family [Action]
passage: Two weeks before the Hindi recitation, I made my family my audience. Every night after dinner, Amma, my aunt Manjula and Dadi sat on the sofa, and I stood by the TV and recited. The first night I raced through all four verses and finished out of breath. Dadi said, "Slow down, my boy. We are not catching a train." Manjula Aunty said, "And look at us, Sachin, not at the floor." It was hard. When I looked up I forgot words. But each night I went a bit slower and lifted my eyes a bit more. On the day, I saw the judges' faces and didn't panic, because I'd practised looking at faces all week.

qa.q: Who sat on the sofa as Sachin's audience?
qa.a: Amma, Manjula Aunty and Dadi sat on the sofa.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel after racing through the first night?
qa.a: Sachin felt out of breath and flustered, and looking up at first made the words slip away.

subtype: Approach: imagining the stage and how he will walk in [Thinking]
passage: The night before the Republic Day speech, I couldn't sleep, so I tried what my sister Jasleen does before exams. I closed my eyes and pictured it all. The side curtain, the smell of dust on the stage. My name being called: "Gautam, Class 5." Walking out, ten steps, to the chalk cross in the middle. Turning. Looking at the back wall, where the clock is. Breathing in. Saying the first line: "Good morning, respected Principal." I did it three times, each time slower. When I opened my eyes, my heart was still thumping, but the stage felt like somewhere I had already been. Next morning, when they called my name, my feet already knew the ten steps.

qa.q: How many steps did Gautam picture from the curtain to the chalk cross?
qa.a: Gautam pictured ten steps to the chalk cross.

qa.a: Gautam still felt nervous, with a thumping heart, but calmer and more familiar with the stage.

Sumit is one of our narrators and has been very nervous at rehearsals. Yesterday I found him sitting behind the stage with his eyes closed and his lips moving. I thought he was praying. His voice was clearer than in any rehearsal so far. Today I let the whole narrators' group sit for two quiet minutes before the run-through to picture their entrances. Sumit showed the others how.

subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage: Our school choir sang at the district festival last month, and I had a solo, two verses. I loved the first verse. It had a high note that made my arms tingle, so I sang it everywhere: in the bath, walking to school, while Amma cooked. The second verse was harder, so I kept thinking, "Later." My little brother Hrithik even knew verse one by heart and sang it back to me. On the day I walked out and sang verse one perfectly. Then the music went on, and my mouth opened, and nothing was there. Rukmini, the girl who knew every note of verse one, stood in silence. The choir teacher started singing with me. My face burned all afternoon.

qa.q: Who knew verse one by heart and sang it back to Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini's little brother Hrithik knew verse one by heart.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when the second verse was not there?
qa.a: Rukmini felt shocked and deeply embarrassed, with a burning face all afternoon.

qa.a: Practise the hard second verse first each day, because the part you avoid is the part most likely to break under pressure.

qa.q: How might the moment have looked to the choir teacher?
qa.a: The choir teacher saw a strong start and then silence, and quickly sang along to help; it was probably a worried moment.

grounding: It shows a girl practising only the verse she enjoys, being confident at first on stage and then forgetting the second verse she barely practised.

subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
passage:
Music teacher's note, after the inter-house singing
Preeti's first verse today was the best I've heard from her. She had clearly practised it many times; she even closed her eyes on the long note. Then the second verse began, and she stopped. She looked at me with wide eyes, and I mouthed the first words. She caught up halfway through, quietly. Afterwards she told me she had sung verse one "a hundred times" because she loved it, and verse two only twice. She was very upset. I told her the slip did not undo the lovely first verse. From next week, our practice rule will be: start with the verse you know least. I have told Irfan, her house captain, too.
- Music teacher

subtype: Approach: worrying so much that he stops practising [Pitfall]
passage: When Miss chose me for the class skit, I was happy for about one hour. Then I started imagining the hall full, everyone watching, someone laughing when I said my line wrong. My stomach churned. So I didn't practise. Every time Amma said, "Pema, let's do your lines," I said I had homework. If I didn't look at the script, I didn't have to feel it. But the day got closer, and I knew my lines less, so I felt worse, so I practised even less. My sister Aparna called it the worry circle. Two days before the show, she sat on my bed and said, "Read one line to me, bhai. Just one." I did. My hands shook.

qa.q: What did Aparna call the pattern?
qa.a: Aparna called it the worry circle.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when imagining the full hall?
qa.a: Pema felt afraid of being laughed at, with a churning stomach, and avoided the script to escape that feeling.

qa.q: What would you change first to break the worry circle, and why?
qa.a: Start with one line a day to someone kind, like Aparna, because a tiny, safe step lowers the fear so practice can grow.

qa.q: How does Pema's avoiding look to Amma?
qa.a: Amma keeps offering help and hears only "homework", so she may feel puzzled and a little worried.

grounding: It shows a boy so afraid of being laughed at that he avoids rehearsing, which makes him more nervous in a growing cycle.

Class teacher's note, Class 3B, drama week
Divyansh has a short speaking part in our class play. For two weeks he has found reasons to miss rehearsal: a headache, a lost script, a trip to the washroom. Today I found him in the corridor, pale, and he said, "Ma'am, what if they laugh at me?" He had not practised at home either. I think the less he rehearses, the more frightened he gets, and the more frightened he gets, the less he rehearses. I sat with him for five minutes and we read his three lines together, quietly. Tomorrow I will let him rehearse alone with me first, then with two friends, then with the class. I have also called his mother.
- Usha

"Sudha, your hands are shaking."
"Vishal sir, I can't. Everyone's out there."
"Remember what we did in class? Show me. Hand on your tummy."
"In, two, three, four."
"Good. Out."
"Out, two, three, four."
"Again."
"In, two, three, four... out, two, three, four."
"How's the heart?"
"Still fast."
"Twice more."
Sudha breathed, eyes on the curtain rope.
"Now?"
"Slower." She held up her hand. "Not shaking."
"That's it. Take your spot."
The music began, and Sudha walked on counting her first eight steps.

subtype: Approach: calming with slow breaths before going on [Action]
passage: Before our Bihu dance at the school function, I thought I was going to be sick with nerves. My friend Devika, who dances next to me, grabbed my arm backstage. "Jasleen, the breathing," she whispered. Our dance teacher had taught all of us girls in the group: breathe in for four, out for four, with a hand on your stomach. We did it together, looking at each other. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four. The first time, my heart was still racing. The fourth time, I could feel it slow down, and my hands stopped fiddling with my dupatta. When the drum began, I walked out steady. Now I do it before tests as well.

qa.a: Jasleen's hands stopped fiddling with the dupatta.

Saturday: On stage, Nazia's second line vanished. She paused, took a breath, and looked at Chaitanya. He whispered, "The river..." She picked it up. The audience never knew.

Look at the squirrel, my friend Kamla, who had the line after mine. On the day, it happened. Halfway through, blank. I stopped. Breathed. Looked at Kamla. She mouthed "carrots", and it all came back. Friday
Today I recorded my speech for the Science Day assembly on Mummy's phone, just to hear it. BIG mistake. Or maybe not. I sounded like a train with no brakes. And at the end of each sentence my voice went down into a mumble. Suraj bhaiya listened and said, "What was that last word, little brother? Mmmmfff?" I was annoyed, but he was right. So I tried again. This time I paused after every sentence, counted one in my head, and said the last word as loudly as the first. Then I played both recordings one after the other. The second one sounded like a real speech. I'm going to do it once more tomorrow.
- Harish

subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
passage: In the small school at Nandgaon, Manjula ma'am had chosen Wasim to give the welcome speech on Independence Day. He was racing, and the end of every sentence disappeared. "Wel-come-to-our-guests-mmm." His Ammi laughed from the doorway, and he laughed too. He tried again, slowly, stopping to breathe after each sentence and ending each one clearly. He played the two recordings back to back. The second sounded like a grown-up. The next day he showed Manjula ma'am both, and she said, "Now I can hear every word."

subtype: Approach: continuing smoothly after a mistake on stage [Revision]
passage: The school auditorium was packed for Annual Day, and Sarika's group was fourth. Halfway through the folk dance, she turned left when everyone turned right. For one beat she stood facing Hansa, nose to nose. Her face went hot. Then she smiled, as if it was part of the dance, spun round, caught the drumbeat and joined the next clap with the others. Backstage she sat down hard on a bench. "Everyone saw!" Hansa shook her head. "My mother didn't. I asked her in the interval." The dance teacher came by. "That smile saved it. Most people saw a girl enjoying herself." Sarika laughed, still shaky.

subtype: Approach: continuing smoothly after a mistake on stage [Revision]
